## What popcorn does

Population-scale single-cell RNA-seq makes it possible to estimate not
just one pooled gene co-expression network, but a separate network for
every donor in a study. A donor-specific correlation estimated from a
few hundred cells is noisy, so a difference between two donors at a
given gene pair can reflect sampling noise rather than real biological
heterogeneity.

popcorn is a two-stage framework for estimating reliable donor-level
co-expression:

1. **Stage 1** fits a covariate-adjusted marginal model to each gene
   (negative binomial by default) and converts each gene's counts to a
   Gaussian-copula score, from which it computes a global correlation
   (all cells pooled) and each donor's own raw correlation.
2. **Stage 2** applies a random-effects variance decomposition that
   separates genuine between-donor heterogeneity from sampling noise at
   each gene pair, and adaptively shrinks each donor's noisy raw
   correlation toward the global correlation by a ratio set by that
   edge's estimated heterogeneity relative to the donor's own sampling
   variance.

This vignette runs the full pipeline, end to end, on a small simulated
toy dataset -- not any of the real cohorts analyzed in the associated
paper -- to show what popcorn's input and output look like.

```{r setup}
library(popcorn)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(SingleCellExperiment))
```

## A toy dataset

We simulate `r 4000` cells from `r 20` donors and `r 5` genes, using the
same construction as the simulations in the associated paper (see its
Methods): for each donor, draw Gaussian scores from a
donor-specific correlation matrix, map them to the uniform scale, then
quantile-transform to a negative binomial count whose mean depends on
each cell's (simulated) library size.

Four of the five genes share one correlation structure across every
donor (no real donor-to-donor heterogeneity at those edges). The
`g1`-`g2` edge is the exception: each donor's true correlation is an
independent draw from a Normal distribution on the Fisher-z scale
around a global value, `atanh(0.2)`, with variance `tau2_true = 0.05`
-- the same mechanism the paper's simulations use to inject
heterogeneity (random donor effects `u_de ~ N(0, tau2_e_true)` around a
global correlation), not a hand-picked pattern.

```{r simulate-data}
set.seed(42)
G <- 5
donors <- paste0("D", 1:20)
n_cells_per_donor <- 200
D <- length(donors)
N <- D * n_cells_per_donor
gene_names <- paste0("g", 1:G)

donor_id <- rep(donors, each = n_cells_per_donor)
log1p_total_counts <- rnorm(N, mean = 7, sd = 0.3)

# Shared ground-truth correlation: same for every donor at every edge
# except g1-g2 (set per donor below).
C_shared <- diag(G)
C_shared[3, 4] <- C_shared[4, 3] <- 0.4

# g1-g2: real donor-to-donor heterogeneity, drawn the same way the
# paper's simulations inject it (u_de ~ N(0, tau2_e_true), added to the
# global Fisher-z value) -- not a hand-picked two-value pattern.
z_global_g1g2  <- fisher_z(0.2)
tau2_true_g1g2 <- 0.05
u_de           <- rnorm(D, mean = 0, sd = sqrt(tau2_true_g1g2))
heterog_group  <- inv_fisher_z(z_global_g1g2 + u_de)
names(heterog_group) <- donors

mu_base <- c(30, 25, 40, 35, 20)
theta_g <- c(4, 5, 6, 4, 5)

counts <- matrix(0L, nrow = G, ncol = N, dimnames = list(gene_names, NULL))
for (d in donors) {
  idx_d <- which(donor_id == d)
  C_d <- C_shared
  C_d[1, 2] <- C_d[2, 1] <- heterog_group[d]
  Z_d <- matrix(rnorm(length(idx_d) * G), nrow = length(idx_d), ncol = G) %*% chol(C_d)
  U_d <- pnorm(Z_d)
  for (g in seq_len(G)) {
    mu_dig <- mu_base[g] * exp(log1p_total_counts[idx_d] - mean(log1p_total_counts))
    counts[g, idx_d] <- qnbinom(U_d[, g], mu = mu_dig, size = theta_g[g])
  }
}
```

Each gene's counts are negative binomial, `NB(mu_dig, theta_g[g])`:
`mu_base[g]` is the gene's baseline mean count (at the average cell's
library size), scaled per cell by that cell's own
`log1p_total_counts`; `theta_g[g]` is the gene's dispersion (smaller
means more over-dispersed relative to a Poisson with the same mean).
Both are set by hand here, not fit from real data:

```{r gene-params}
data.frame(
  gene = gene_names,
  mu_base = mu_base,
  theta_g = theta_g,
  empirical_mean = round(rowMeans(counts), 1),
  empirical_var = round(apply(counts, 1, var), 1)
)
```

popcorn takes a `SingleCellExperiment` as input, with covariates in
`colData()`:

```{r build-sce}
cell_meta <- data.frame(
  Donor = donor_id,
  log1p_total_counts = log1p_total_counts,
  row.names = paste0("cell", seq_len(N))
)
colnames(counts) <- rownames(cell_meta)
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = counts), colData = cell_meta)
sce
```

## Running the pipeline

`run_coexp_pipeline()` runs both stages and writes every intermediate
and final result under `comb_path`. We use a temporary directory here;
in practice this should be a persistent location, since Stage 1's
per-gene fits are the most expensive step and are cached (re-running
with the same `comb_path` skips genes already fit).

By default popcorn uses the asymptotic chi-squared null for the
heterogeneity test (`evidence_p_method = "Q0_DL"`, used throughout the
associated paper) and skips the simulation-based
pseudo-donor null (`compute_Q0_sim = FALSE`). We set both explicitly
below for clarity. If you do set `compute_Q0_sim = TRUE`, pseudo-donors
are formed by partitioning cells into disjoint groups
(`pseudo_donor_mode = "permutation"`), and setting
`evidence_p_method = "Q0_sim"` without `compute_Q0_sim = TRUE` is an
error rather than silently returning `NA` p-values.

```{r run-pipeline, results = "hide"}
comb_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "popcorn_vignette_demo")

# Clear any earlier output at comb_path, so this chunk can be re-run after
# changing the simulated dataset above (run_marginal_stage() refuses to
# reuse a comb_path cached for a different sce).
unlink(comb_path, recursive = TRUE)

res <- run_coexp_pipeline(
  sce = sce,
  comb_path = comb_path,
  gene_names = gene_names,
  covariates = "log1p_total_counts",
  mu_formula = "log1p_total_counts",
  sigma_formula = "1",
  family_use = "nb",
  donor_col = "Donor",
  n_cores_marginal = 1,
  n_cores_split = 1,
  n_cores_ewvds = 1,
  donors = donors,
  compute_Q0_sim = FALSE,
  evidence_p_method = "Q0_DL",
  do_estimate_lfdr = FALSE,
  pipeline_tag = "vignette_demo"
)
```

## Inspecting the output

The main result is saved to `EWVDS_result.rds` under a
`donor_network_EWVDS_<pipeline_tag>` subdirectory of `comb_path`. Its
`edge_df` summarizes every gene pair's estimated donor heterogeneity,
`tau2_e`, and the corresponding heterogeneity test p-value, `p_Q_e`.
Because this is simulated data, we also know each edge's *true*
between-donor heterogeneity, `true_tau2`, to check `tau2_e` against:
for `g1`-`g2` this is the sample variance (Fisher-z scale, matching
`tau2_e`'s own scale) of its 20 actual per-donor draws -- close to, but
not exactly, the generating `tau2_true_g1g2 = 0.05`, since it is itself
only a 20-donor estimate of that parameter; for every other edge, the
true correlation is identical across donors by construction, so
`true_tau2` is exactly `0`.

```{r inspect-result}
result <- readRDS(file.path(comb_path, "donor_network_EWVDS_vignette_demo", "EWVDS_result.rds"))

true_tau2 <- function(gene_a, gene_b) {
  if (gene_a == "g1" && gene_b == "g2") return(var(fisher_z(heterog_group)))
  0
}
result$edge_df$true_tau2 <- mapply(true_tau2, result$edge_df$gene1, result$edge_df$gene2)

result$edge_df[order(-result$edge_df$tau2_e), c("gene1", "gene2", "true_tau2", "tau2_e", "p_Q_e")]
```

`g1`-`g2` -- the one edge with real, injected donor heterogeneity --
has by far the largest `true_tau2` and `tau2_e`, and the smallest
`p_Q_e`, exactly as intended, and `tau2_e` recovers `true_tau2`
reasonably well. Every other edge's `true_tau2` is `0`, and `tau2_e`
is at or near `0` too.

### True vs. estimated correlation

Because this toy dataset is simulated, we know the *true* per-donor
correlation that generated it. Following the recovery-plot style
of the associated paper (one representative null edge and one
representative signal edge, true vs. estimated correlation across
donors), we pick one representative null edge (`g1`-`g3`) and
the one edge with real donor heterogeneity (`g1`-`g2`), and for each,
plot every donor's true correlation against its raw and its shrunk
estimate side by side:

```{r raw-correlation-helper}
raw_correlation <- function(gene_a, gene_b) {
  vapply(donors, function(d) {
    Sigma_d <- as.matrix(read.csv(file.path(comb_path, "donors", d, "Sigma_Z.csv"),
                                   row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE))
    Sigma_d[gene_a, gene_b]
  }, numeric(1))
}

true_correlation <- function(gene_a, gene_b, donor) {
  if (gene_a == "g1" && gene_b == "g2") return(unname(heterog_group[donor]))
  C_shared[match(gene_a, gene_names), match(gene_b, gene_names)]
}

edge_df <- result$edge_df
true_mat <- raw_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow(edge_df), length(donors), dimnames = list(NULL, donors))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(edge_df))) {
  ga <- edge_df$gene1[i]; gb <- edge_df$gene2[i]
  raw_mat[i, ] <- raw_correlation(ga, gb)
  for (d in donors) true_mat[i, d] <- true_correlation(ga, gb, d)
}
shrunk_mat <- result$R_DL_mat
```

```{r true-vs-estimated, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 12}
plot_recovery_grid <- function(edge_row, row_label,
                                main_cex = 1, axis_label_cex = 1,
                                axis_tick_cex = 1, annotation_cex = 0.85) {
  true_vals <- true_mat[edge_row, ]

  panel <- function(est_vals, main) {
    plot(true_vals, est_vals, pch = 16, col = "steelblue",
         xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1),
         xlab = "true correlation", ylab = "estimated correlation", main = main,
         cex.main = main_cex, cex.lab = axis_label_cex, cex.axis = axis_tick_cex)
    abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "red")
    # r is undefined (NA) when true_vals has zero variance, e.g. a null edge
    # whose true correlation is the same constant for every donor -- not a
    # computation error, just say so instead of printing a bare "NA".
    r_val    <- if (sd(true_vals) > 0) cor(true_vals, est_vals) else NA_real_
    r_label  <- if (is.na(r_val)) "r = NA (true value constant)" else sprintf("r = %.3f", r_val)
    rmse_val <- sqrt(mean((true_vals - est_vals)^2))
    usr <- par("usr")
    text(usr[1] + 0.03 * diff(usr[1:2]), usr[4] - 0.05 * diff(usr[3:4]),
         labels = sprintf("%s\nRMSE = %.3f", r_label, rmse_val), adj = c(0, 1), cex = annotation_cex)
  }

  panel(raw_mat[edge_row, ],    sprintf("%s -- raw", row_label))
  panel(shrunk_mat[edge_row, ], sprintf("%s -- shrunk", row_label))
}

null_edge_row   <- which(edge_df$gene1 == "g1" & edge_df$gene2 == "g3")
signal_edge_row <- which(edge_df$gene1 == "g1" & edge_df$gene2 == "g2")

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), mgp = c(3, 0.8, 0))
plot_recovery_grid(null_edge_row,   "null edge (g1-g3)",
                    main_cex = 2, axis_label_cex = 2, axis_tick_cex = 2, annotation_cex = 2)
plot_recovery_grid(signal_edge_row, "signal edge (g1-g2)",
                    main_cex = 2, axis_label_cex = 2, axis_tick_cex = 2, annotation_cex = 2)
par(old_par)
```

For both edges, the shrunk estimate's points sit closer to the `y = x`
line than raw's, with a higher `r` and lower `RMSE` -- most dramatically
at the null edge, where the raw correlation scatters widely around `0`
purely from per-donor sampling noise and shrinkage pulls it back in; at
the signal edge, both track the true, donor-specific value reasonably
well, since there is genuine heterogeneity there to recover rather than
noise to remove. The table below aggregates this same raw-vs-shrunk RMSE
comparison across every edge and donor, not just these two examples:

```{r rmse-summary}
rmse <- function(est) sqrt(mean((as.vector(true_mat) - as.vector(est))^2))
data.frame(estimator = c("raw", "popcorn"), rmse = c(rmse(raw_mat), rmse(shrunk_mat)))
```

## Recommended usage for real data

The toy example above relies on `run_coexp_pipeline()`'s defaults
(`covariates = "log1p_total_counts"`, `mu_formula = "log1p_total_counts"`)
to get running with minimal setup. For real data, we recommend adjusting
for technical and compositional covariates more fully -- this is the
configuration used to produce the associated paper's results:

```{r recommended-usage, eval = FALSE}
# Illustrative only -- not run here. `sce` should already be subset to
# a single cell type, with `counts` holding raw UMI counts and
# `colData()` holding `log1p_total_counts` and `Donor`.
run_coexp_pipeline(
  sce           = sce,
  comb_path     = "path/to/output/",
  covariates    = c("log1p_total_counts", "Donor"),
  mu_formula    = "log1p_total_counts + Donor",
  sigma_formula = "1",
  family_use    = "nb",
  donor_col     = "Donor"
)
```

`log1p_total_counts` adjusts for per-cell technical noise (library
size); including `Donor` in `mu_formula` additionally adjusts the mean
model itself for between-donor compositional differences, on top of
Stage 2's own between-donor heterogeneity estimation.
`noise_method`, `null_method`, `pseudo_donor_mode`, `compute_Q0_sim`,
`evidence_p_method`, and `excess_variance_method` already default to the settings used
throughout the associated paper, so they don't need to be set explicitly
unless you want to change them. `celltype` never needs to be set
either way -- see `?run_marginal_stage`.

## A note on reproducibility

popcorn's Stage 1 marginal fit uses a randomized probability-integral
transform, so two unseeded runs on the same data give slightly
different results. This is a deliberate statistical design choice, not
a bug, and its effect on the final shrunk estimate is small relative to
real heterogeneous edges. Pass `seed` to `run_coexp_pipeline()` (or
`run_marginal_stage()`) to make a run exactly reproducible, including
across repeated calls in one R session and across `n_cores_marginal`.
A bare `set.seed()` before the call is enough only in a fresh R
session, because the `parallel` package keeps the random-number stream
it hands to forked workers across calls (see `?run_marginal_stage`).
The results reported in the associated paper were generated before
this option existed, so they can be reproduced only up to this small
run-to-run variability. The paper's analysis code
(<https://github.com/keleslab/popcorn-paper>) uses popcorn 0.1.1.
